slides.headline: Choosing a fix, in one sentence
slides.body: List every fix that would repair the root cause, rank them by what each can destroy and how each is undone, and take the one that only adds.

slides.headline: Precisely
slides.body: Rank by five questions, in this order.

items: Does it destroy uncommitted work? That work has no object and no reflog. Anything that can remove it, git reset --hard, git restore, git clean, git stash drop, every --abort, ranks last unless the working tree is clean or copied.
Does it rewrite commits that another repository has? Rewriting published history turns one person's problem into every clone's problem.
Does it change the server? A local change is undone locally. A push, a deleted remote branch or a changed rule is seen by others and may start workflows.
Is it undone by one command? A new commit is undone by a revert; a moved ref by moving it back; a pruned object by nothing.
Can it be previewed? --dry-run, git merge-tree, git diff <target>, git log <range>, or a rehearsal in a copy.

slides.headline: Three rules of thumb
slides.body: On a shared branch, undo with git revert, not with git reset, which moves the branch to another commit.

slides.headline: Three rules of thumb
slides.body: When a ref must move back, use git reset --keep.

slides.headline: Three rules of thumb
slides.body: When a force push, which overwrites the server's branch, is the correct fix, state the expected old value: git push --force-with-lease=<branch>:<expected-id>.

slides.headline: Verification, in one sentence
slides.body: A fix is verified when the commands that showed the problem now show its absence, for the reason you predicted, in every place the problem existed.

items: The symptom. Repeat the command or page that showed it: the rejected push succeeds; the pull request lists the expected commits.
The state. Repeat the diagnosis commands that exposed the cause. The first line of git status changed; the brackets in git branch -vv changed; .git has no state files.

Every copy. Compare IDs, not names: git rev-parse HEAD @{upstream} and git ls-remote origin <branch> must print the same ID. Then the colleague's clone, the pull request, the pipeline run for that exact commit.
Nothing else changed. git diff <backup> HEAD or git range-diff shows that the result differs from the preserved state only where intended. git fsck reports no damage. git status shows no leftovers.

slides.headline: What a pull request needs after a fix
slides.body: is platform behavior: a push to the head branch reruns workflows and can dismiss approvals.

slides.headline: The symptom catalog
slides.body: Twenty-six symptoms in five groups.

rows: A commit is missing

(a) it is on another branch; (b) it was made on a detached HEAD or inside a stopped operation; (c) a reset, rebase or amend took it off the branch; (d) it was never pushed, or pushed to another branch; (e) it was never made: the change was not staged
git branch -a --contains <id>; git status (first line); git reflog, git reflog show <branch>; git ls-remote origin; git log --all --oneline -- <path>
A push is rejected

(a) ! [rejected] (fetch first) or (non-fast-forward): the server's branch has commits you lack; (b) the pull integrates another branch than the push targets; (c) ! [remote rejected]: a rule, a hook, push protection or a file-size limit, named in the remote: lines; (d) no permission
Read the bracket and the reason in the push output; git fetch, git status -sb; git branch -vv; gh ruleset check <branch>
A pull request shows hundreds of changes

(a) the wrong base branch; (b) the head branch was reused after a squash merge; (c) the branch was rebased or force-pushed; (d) every line changed: line endings or a formatter; (e) a lock file or generated file
git log --oneline <base>..<head>; git diff --stat <base>...<head>; git merge-base <base> <head>; git diff --ignore-cr-at-eol --stat <base>...<head>

slides.headline: The pattern across the catalog
slides.body: The textbook calls it the content of the book in one line: nearly every symptom is a difference between two of the places of the state table that someone assumed were equal.

slides.headline: When not to use the full method
slides.body: A message that names its own remedy, and whose remedy is green, needs no hypothesis table: "The current branch has no upstream branch", with the command printed beneath it, or a typo in a branch name.

slides.headline: When to stop and escalate
slides.body: If the evidence shows a credential in history, stop diagnosing and start the secret response: revoke first, investigate second.

rows: A "fix" is typed before the state is known
The reflog shows reset, checkout or rebase (abort) entries made after the report
Nothing but green commands until the root cause is written down
The diagnosis uses stale remote-tracking refs
git status says "up to date" and git ls-remote origin shows another ID
Treat origin/<branch> as "the server at the last fetch"
The wrong layer is blamed
"GitHub lost my commits" while git ls-remote shows the server never had them
The label "Git, GitHub or Actions" is a required line of every explanation
The evidence is destroyed by the investigation
The reflog was expired, a branch was deleted "to tidy up", git gc was run
Preserve before phase 3; never run git gc or git prune during an incident

slides.body: A picture helps. The ladder is a physical picture, and it works as one.
Where the picture breaks: on a real ladder the rungs are equally spaced.
For verification, think of a doctor who ends a treatment.

slides.direction: The ladder of section 29.9. Build it from the bottom rung, number 1, upward, and say the right-hand column aloud for each rung.
slides.text:
1  add a ref                 git branch, git tag, git update-ref               nothing can be lost
  2  add a commit              git commit, git revert, git cherry-pick, merge    undone by a revert or by moving the ref back
  3  move a local ref          git reset --keep, git branch -f, git rebase       undone through the reflog or a backup ref
  4  overwrite the work tree   git reset --hard, git restore, git clean          uncommitted work is unrecoverable
  5  rewrite the server        git push --force-with-lease=<ref>:<expected>      others must repair their clones
  6  remove the safety net     git reflog expire, git gc --prune=now             nothing undoes it

slides.body: Five mistakes to watch for.

items: Choosing the fix you know instead of the lowest rung. Root cause: the candidates were never listed and ranked by what each can destroy.
Using git reset --hard where --keep would do. Root cause: --hard overwrites files with local changes, and uncommitted work has no object and no reflog.
Stopping at "the symptom is gone". Root cause: a fix in one clone is not a fix on the server, in the pull request or in the pipeline, so the first check can pass while a later one fails.
Comparing names instead of IDs. Root cause: origin/<branch> is the server at the last fetch; only an ID from git ls-remote says what the server holds now.
Reading a verification command without its limits. Root cause: a patch-ID comparison reports a port that needed conflict resolution as missing, so the mark alone can mislead.

slides.body: Now, out of the lab. The engineer from the hook does the four checks before she goes to bed.

She previews the push, pushes, compares the three IDs again, and opens the pull request for the release: the push has rerun the workflows, and one approval was dismissed, which she notes for the morning.

beats.text: Choosing a fix, in one sentence. List every fix that would repair the root cause, rank them by what each can destroy and how each is undone, and take the one that only adds.
beats.tele: Choosing a fix, in one sentence. List every fix that would repair the root cause, rank them by what each can destroy and how each is undone, and take the one that only adds.

beats.text: Precisely. Rank by five questions, in this order.
beats.tele: Precisely. Rank by five questions, in this order.

beats.text: Does it destroy uncommitted work? That work has no object and no reflog. Anything that can remove it, git reset --hard, git restore, git clean, git stash drop, every --abort, ranks last unless the working tree is clean or copied.
beats.tele: Does it destroy uncommitted work? That work has no object and no reflog. Anything that can remove it, `git reset --hard`, `git restore`, `git clean`, `git stash drop`, every `--abort`, ranks last unless the working tree is clean or copied.

beats.text: Does it rewrite commits that another repository has? Rewriting published history turns one person's problem into every clone's problem.
beats.tele: Does it rewrite commits that another repository has? Rewriting published history turns one person's problem into every clone's problem.

beats.text: Does it change the server? A local change is undone locally. A push, a deleted remote branch or a changed rule is seen by others and may start workflows.
beats.tele: Does it change the server? A local change is undone locally. A push, a deleted remote branch or a changed rule is seen by others and may start workflows.

beats.text: Is it undone by one command? A new commit is undone by a revert; a moved ref by moving it back; a pruned object by nothing.
beats.tele: Is it undone by one command? A new commit is undone by a revert; a moved ref by moving it back; a pruned object by nothing.

beats.text: Can it be previewed? --dry-run, git merge-tree, git diff <target>, git log <range>, or a rehearsal in a copy.
beats.tele: Can it be previewed? `--dry-run`, `git merge-tree`, `git diff <target>`, `git log <range>`, or a rehearsal in a copy.

beats.text: The result is a ladder of six rungs, which is today's diagram. Prefer the lowest rung that repairs the cause. In the case of video 180 that was rungs 1 and 2. In the case of video 181 it was rung 3, on commits that existed nowhere else, with rung 1 first.
beats.tele: The result is a ladder of six rungs, which is today's diagram. Prefer the lowest rung that repairs the cause. In the case of video 180 that was rungs 1 and 2. In the case of video 181 it was rung 3, on commits that existed nowhere else, with rung 1 first.

beats.text: Three rules of thumb.
beats.tele: Three rules of thumb.

beats.text: On a shared branch, undo with git revert, not with git reset, which moves the branch to another commit. A revert adds a commit. Everyone's next pull is a fast-forward, a plain move ahead.
beats.tele: On a shared branch, undo with `git revert`, not with `git reset`, which moves the branch to another commit. A revert adds a commit. Everyone's next pull is a fast-forward, a plain move ahead.

beats.text: When a ref must move back, use git reset --keep. It refuses when a file with local changes would be overwritten, where --hard overwrites it.
beats.tele: When a ref must move back, use `git reset --keep`. It refuses when a file with local changes would be overwritten, where `--hard` overwrites it.

beats.text: When a force push, which overwrites the server's branch, is the correct fix, state the expected old value: git push --force-with-lease=<branch>:<expected-id>. The bare form is defeated by anything that fetches in the background.
beats.tele: When a force push, which overwrites the server's branch, is the correct fix, state the expected old value: `git push --force-with-lease=<branch>:<expected-id>`. The bare form is defeated by anything that fetches in the background.

beats.text: Verification, in one sentence. A fix is verified when the commands that showed the problem now show its absence, for the reason you predicted, in every place the problem existed.
beats.tele: Verification, in one sentence. A fix is verified when the commands that showed the problem now show its absence, for the reason you predicted, in every place the problem existed.

beats.text: Four checks, in this order.
beats.tele: Four checks, in this order.

beats.text: The symptom. Repeat the command or page that showed it: the rejected push succeeds; the pull request lists the expected commits.
beats.tele: The symptom. Repeat the command or page that showed it: the rejected push succeeds; the pull request lists the expected commits.

beats.text: The state. Repeat the diagnosis commands that exposed the cause. The first line of git status changed; the brackets in git branch -vv changed; .git has no state files.
beats.tele: The state. Repeat the diagnosis commands that exposed the cause. The first line of `git status` changed; the brackets in `git branch -vv` changed; `.git` has no state files.

beats.text: Every copy. Compare IDs, not names: git rev-parse HEAD @{upstream} and git ls-remote origin <branch> must print the same ID. Then the colleague's clone, the pull request, the pipeline run for that exact commit.
beats.tele: Every copy. Compare IDs, not names: `git rev-parse HEAD @{upstream}` and `git ls-remote origin <branch>` must print the same ID. Then the colleague's clone, the pull request, the pipeline run for that exact commit.

beats.text: Nothing else changed. git diff <backup> HEAD or git range-diff shows that the result differs from the preserved state only where intended. git fsck reports no damage. git status shows no leftovers.
beats.tele: Nothing else changed. `git diff <backup> HEAD` or `git range-diff` shows that the result differs from the preserved state only where intended. `git fsck` reports no damage. `git status` shows no leftovers.

beats.text: Try it now. Thirty seconds, and it only reads. In the lab shell, or in any repository you have, run git rev-parse HEAD @{upstream}. The upstream is the server branch your branch follows. Do you get two equal IDs? Say what you see.
beats.tele: Try it now. Thirty seconds, and it only reads. In the lab shell, or in any repository you have, run `git rev-parse HEAD @{upstream}`. The upstream is the server branch your branch follows. Do you get two equal IDs? Say what you see.

beats.text: Two equal IDs mean your branch agrees with your record of its upstream. That record is the server at your last fetch, so only git ls-remote tells you what the server holds now. And if Git answered that no upstream is configured, that's a finding too.
beats.tele: Two equal IDs mean your branch agrees with your record of its upstream. That record is the server at your last fetch, so only `git ls-remote` tells you what the server holds now. And if Git answered that no upstream is configured, that's a finding too.

beats.text: Write the prediction before you run the check. Then, and only then, remove what the investigation added: the rescue branch, the evidence directory, the bundle. git branch -D prints the ID, which is one more safety line.
beats.tele: Write the prediction before you run the check. Then, and only then, remove what the investigation added: the rescue branch, the evidence directory, the bundle. `git branch -D` prints the ID, which is one more safety line.

beats.text: What a pull request needs after a fix is platform behavior: a push to the head branch reruns workflows and can dismiss approvals. A forced push marks review comments as outdated. Verification includes reading the pull request page again.
beats.tele: What a pull request needs after a fix is platform behavior: a push to the head branch reruns workflows and can dismiss approvals. A forced push marks review comments as outdated. Verification includes reading the pull request page again.

beats.text: The symptom catalog. Twenty-six symptoms in five groups. History and refs. Working tree and index. Remotes, access and identity. Pull requests, checks and CI. And submodules, LFS and scale. Each row gives the likely causes in the order worth testing, the commands that distinguish them, and the chapter with the mechanism.
beats.tele: The symptom catalog. Twenty-six symptoms in five groups. History and refs. Working tree and index. Remotes, access and identity. Pull requests, checks and CI. And submodules, LFS and scale. Each row gives the likely causes in the order worth testing, the commands that distinguish them, and the chapter with the mechanism.

beats.text: How to use a row: the causes are your ready-made hypotheses, already more than three, and each command is the test that separates them. The catalog doesn't replace the opening ritual. It replaces the blank page after it.
beats.tele: How to use a row: the causes are your ready-made hypotheses, already more than three, and each command is the test that separates them. The catalog doesn't replace the opening ritual. It replaces the blank page after it.

beats.text: The pattern across the catalog. The textbook calls it the content of the book in one line: nearly every symptom is a difference between two of the places of the state table that someone assumed were equal. The working tree and the commit. The branch and HEAD. The local branch and its upstream. The remote-tracking branch and the server. The branch and the merge ref. The diagnosis is finding which two.
beats.tele: The pattern across the catalog. The working tree and the commit. The branch and HEAD. The local branch and its upstream. The remote-tracking branch and the server. The branch and the merge ref. The diagnosis is finding which two.

beats.text: When not to use the full method. A message that names its own remedy, and whose remedy is green, needs no hypothesis table: "The current branch has no upstream branch", with the command printed beneath it, or a typo in a branch name. Run git status, do what the message says, and move on. The full method is for symptoms that contradict what the reporter believes about the state. The opening ritual is never skipped: it takes less than a minute.
beats.tele: When not to use the full method. A message that names its own remedy, and whose remedy is green, needs no hypothesis table: "The current branch has no upstream branch", with the command printed beneath it, or a typo in a branch name. Run `git status`, do what the message says, and move on. The full method is for symptoms that contradict what the reporter believes about the state. The opening ritual is never skipped: it takes less than a minute.

beats.text: When to stop and escalate. If the evidence shows a credential in history, stop diagnosing and start the secret response: revoke first, investigate second. If the repository reports corrupt or missing objects, don't continue working in it: copy it and follow the procedure of Chapter 13. If production is down, restore service first and diagnose afterwards on preserved evidence.
beats.tele: When to stop and escalate. If the evidence shows a credential in history, stop diagnosing and start the secret response: revoke first, investigate second. If the repository reports corrupt or missing objects, don't continue working in it: copy it and follow the procedure of Chapter 13. If production is down, restore service first and diagnose afterwards on preserved evidence.

beats.text: How the method itself fails.
beats.tele: How the method itself fails.

beats.text: A picture helps. The ladder is a physical picture, and it works as one. You climb only as high as the repair requires, and each rung up is further to fall. On the first rung nothing can be lost. On the sixth, nothing can be undone.
beats.tele: A picture helps. The ladder is a physical picture, and it works as one. You climb only as high as the repair requires, and each rung up is further to fall. On the first rung nothing can be lost. On the sixth, nothing can be undone.

beats.text: Where the picture breaks: on a real ladder the rungs are equally spaced. Here the gap between rung 3 and rung 4 is much larger than the others, because it's the gap between "undone through the reflog" and "unrecoverable". The reflog is Git's local record of where each ref has been. And the gap between 4 and 5 is of a different kind: from your own loss to other people's.
beats.tele: Where the picture breaks: on a real ladder the rungs are equally spaced. Here the gap between rung 3 and rung 4 is much larger than the others, because it's the gap between "undone through the reflog" and "unrecoverable". The reflog is Git's local record of where each ref has been. And the gap between 4 and 5 is of a different kind: from your own loss to other people's.

beats.text: For verification, think of a doctor who ends a treatment. The patient says the pain is gone: the symptom. The test that showed the cause is repeated: the state. Both lungs are checked, not one: every copy. And nothing else was harmed by the treatment: nothing else changed. A doctor who stops at the first check has asked the patient, not examined them.
beats.tele: For verification, think of a doctor who ends a treatment. The patient says the pain is gone: the symptom. The test that showed the cause is repeated: the state. Both lungs are checked, not one: every copy. And nothing else was harmed by the treatment: nothing else changed. A doctor who stops at the first check has asked the patient, not examined them.

beats.text: Then place the interview question's five fixes on it as a preview: each has a rung. I won't say which. That's the question.
beats.tele: Then place the interview question's five fixes on it as a preview: each has a rung. I won't say which. That's the question.

beats.text: Choosing. Put the candidates on the ladder before running anything. Continue the cherry-pick with the colleague's resolution: rung 2, it adds commits. Abort and start again: an abort discards the uncommitted resolution, which exists in no object. The note says the operation was intended and gives the intended result, so the resolution can be checked against it. Continue is the lowest rung that repairs the cause.
beats.tele: Choosing. Put the candidates on the ladder before running anything. Continue the cherry-pick with the colleague's resolution: rung 2, it adds commits. Abort and start again: an abort discards the uncommitted resolution, which exists in no object. The note says the operation was intended and gives the intended result, so the resolution can be checked against it. Continue is the lowest rung that repairs the cause.

beats.text: The fix. 🟡 CAUTION: git cherry-pick --continue adds commits to the current branch. Preview: read the resolved file against the note first.
beats.tele: The fix. 🟡 CAUTION: `git cherry-pick --continue` adds commits to the current branch. Preview: read the resolved file against the note first.

beats.text: The file says 0.50 and 128, as the note requires. Staging it marks the conflict resolved. The sequencer, Git's record of the picks that remain, then commits the stopped pick and applies the remaining one: two new commits.
beats.tele: The file says 0.50 and 128, as the note requires. Staging it marks the conflict resolved. The sequencer, Git's record of the picks that remain, then commits the stopped pick and applies the remaining one: two new commits.

beats.text: Verify. Predict before the output: in git cherry -v release/1.4 main, which commits of main will carry a minus sign and which a plus sign, and why? Say it out loud.
beats.tele: Verify. Predict before the output: in `git cherry -v release/1.4 main`, which commits of `main` will carry a minus sign and which a plus sign, and why? Say it out loud.

beats.text: Go through the checks. State: "On branch", clean, and zero state files. The intended result: the committed file has the two values from the note. Then git cherry: two commits of main are marked with a minus sign, present on the release branch in equivalent form. Two are marked with a plus sign. One of them was deliberately not backported. The other, e0631de, was backported, and is marked as missing. Why? Say your explanation out loud.

The other, `e0631de`, was backported, and is marked as missing. Why? Say your explanation out loud.

beats.text: This is the limit of the patch-ID check that you met in video 172. It compares commits by their change, not by their ID, and the port needed a conflict resolution, so its diff differs from the original. A check that passes or fails has to be read with its limits. Here the evidence that the port happened is the commit itself and the handover note.

beats.text: The failure scenario, in the rehearsal copy. What would the other choice have done? 🟡 CAUTION: git cherry-pick --abort resets the index and the working tree to the starting commit.
beats.tele: The failure scenario, in the rehearsal copy. What would the other choice have done? 🟡 CAUTION: `git cherry-pick --abort` resets the index and the working tree to the starting commit.

beats.text: Quick quiz. After the abort, where is the branch? A, on the first pick, the one that had succeeded. B, back before the whole backport. And what does guard.yaml contain? Your answer?
beats.tele: Quick quiz. After the abort, where is the branch? A, on the first pick, the one that had succeeded. B, back before the whole backport. And what does `guard.yaml` contain? Your answer?

beats.text: B. Clean, quiet, and wrong. The branch is back at 329817a, before the whole backport, so even the pick that had already succeeded has left the branch. And the file says 512: the colleague's resolution is gone. It was never in an object, so no reflog has it.

beats.text: The recovery, from what was preserved.
beats.tele: The recovery, from what was preserved.

beats.text: The rescue branch brings back the completed pick with a fast-forward. The cherry-pick is started again and stops at the same conflict. The resolved file comes from the copy of the repository, the one layer that holds uncommitted files. Then continue.

beats.text: Verification of the recovery.
beats.tele: Verification of the recovery.

beats.text: The commit IDs differ from the first repair. The tree IDs, which name the complete snapshots, are equal: both repositories end with the same content. That's the fourth check done precisely: nothing else changed.

beats.text: Say the lesson of the scenario in one sentence: the same mistake was made in the rehearsal that a tired engineer makes at night, and it cost nothing, because two layers of preservation each returned the part they hold.

beats.text: Five mistakes to watch for.
beats.tele: Five mistakes to watch for.

beats.text: Choosing the fix you know instead of the lowest rung. Root cause: the candidates were never listed and ranked by what each can destroy.
beats.tele: Choosing the fix you know instead of the lowest rung. Root cause: the candidates were never listed and ranked by what each can destroy.

beats.text: Using git reset --hard where --keep would do. Root cause: --hard overwrites files with local changes, and uncommitted work has no object and no reflog.
beats.tele: Using `git reset --hard` where `--keep` would do. Root cause: `--hard` overwrites files with local changes, and uncommitted work has no object and no reflog.

beats.text: Stopping at "the symptom is gone". Root cause: a fix in one clone is not a fix on the server, in the pull request or in the pipeline, so the first check can pass while a later one fails.
beats.tele: Stopping at "the symptom is gone". Root cause: a fix in one clone is not a fix on the server, in the pull request or in the pipeline, so the first check can pass while a later one fails.

beats.text: Comparing names instead of IDs. Root cause: origin/<branch> is the server at the last fetch; only an ID from git ls-remote says what the server holds now.
beats.tele: Comparing names instead of IDs. Root cause: `origin/<branch>` is the server at the last fetch; only an ID from `git ls-remote` says what the server holds now.

beats.text: Reading a verification command without its limits. Root cause: a patch-ID comparison reports a port that needed conflict resolution as missing, so the mark alone can mislead.
beats.tele: Reading a verification command without its limits. Root cause: a patch-ID comparison reports a port that needed conflict resolution as missing, so the mark alone can mislead.

beats.text: Now, out of the lab. The engineer from the hook does the four checks before she goes to bed. The symptom: the backported release branch builds. The state: no cherry-pick in progress, clean status. Every copy: git rev-parse HEAD @{upstream} prints two equal IDs, and git ls-remote origin prints a different one for the branch. She hadn't pushed. Check three failed, at eleven at night, with check one green. There's the sentence from the opening, come true.
